---
title: "Quiz: linear deconvolution"
---

Short questions to test your understanding. Try each on paper first, then open the answer. Notation: $G = HF + N$ per frequency; $W$ is the restoration filter, $\hat F = WG$; SNR is signal power over noise power.

---

**Q1.** Without noise the inverse filter restores a blurred image perfectly. Name the two reasons it fails on real data.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
What happens where $|H|$ is small, and where it is zero?
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
Where $|H|$ is small, the noise term $N/H$ is amplified enormously and swamps the image. Where $H = 0$ (beyond the cut-off, or at the zeros of a motion blur) there is nothing to divide by: those frequencies are not in the data at all, and no filter can bring them back.
:::

---

**Q2.** A truncated inverse with a large ε gives a blurred result with ripples next to every edge. Why the ripples?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
What does a sharp cut in frequency look like in space?
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
The truncated inverse keeps frequencies up to a sharp boundary and sets the rest to zero. Multiplying by a sharp cut-off in frequency is convolving with a sinc-like function in space, whose side lobes appear as ripples (ringing) parallel to edges and around bright spots. Wiener and Tikhonov roll off smoothly and ring much less.
:::

---

**Q3.** With SNR = 100, what does the Wiener filter multiply a frequency with $H = 0.5$ by? And one with $H = 0.01$?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
$W = H/(H^2 + 1/\mathrm{SNR})$ for real $H$.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
$H = 0.5$: $0.5/(0.25 + 0.01) = 1.92$, almost the inverse (2). $H = 0.01$: $0.01/(0.0001 + 0.01) = 0.99$, instead of the inverse's 100: Wiener does not try to restore a frequency that is mostly noise.
:::

---

**Q4.** A deconvolved image is covered in fine bright and dark dots. What went wrong, and which setting do you change?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
Fine dots are high frequencies. Which ones are mostly noise?
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
Too little regularisation: the filter amplifies high frequencies where the data are mostly noise. Lower the SNR given to the Wiener filter, raise λ in Tikhonov, or raise ε in the truncated inverse.
:::

---

**Q5.** After deconvolution every bright cell has a dark rim, darker than the background. Name a likely cause.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
What happens if the restoration "undoes" more blur than there was?
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
The PSF used for restoration is wider than the true one: the filter over-sharpens, subtracting too much light around bright objects, which leaves dark halos (and ringing). A sharp frequency cut (truncated inverse) can also give rims. Check the PSF width first.
:::

---

**Q6.** Tikhonov with the energy penalty and λ = 0.25 is applied to an image of a uniform grey area. What happens to its brightness? And with the roughness penalty?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
A uniform image is pure frequency 0, where $H = 1$.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
Energy penalty: the gain at $f = 0$ is $1/(1 + \lambda) = 0.8$, so the grey level drops by 20 %. The roughness penalty (Laplacian) is zero for a constant image, so it does not penalise the mean: the gain at $f = 0$ is exactly 1 and the brightness is kept.
:::

---

**Q7.** Why do FFT-based restorations often show stripes starting at the image border, and what is the usual fix?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
What does the FFT assume lies beyond the right edge?
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
The FFT treats the image as periodic: the right edge is followed by the left edge. If they differ, the model sees a sharp edge at the border and the restoration rings there; also the real blur brought light in from outside the field, which the model attributes to the wrong place. Fix: pad the image, taper the padding smoothly to the mean, restore, then crop.
:::

---

**Q8.** *(math)* Show that Tikhonov with the energy penalty, $\min\|A\mathbf x - \mathbf g\|^2 + \lambda\|\mathbf x\|^2$, gives the same per-frequency gain as the Wiener filter with a flat signal spectrum. What is the relation between λ and the SNR?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
Normal equations, then diagonalise with the Fourier transform.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
The normal equations are $(A^\top A + \lambda I)\mathbf x = A^\top\mathbf g$. For a circular blur, $A$ is diagonal in the Fourier basis with entries $H(f)$, and $A^\top$ has $H^*(f)$, so $\hat X = H^* G/(|H|^2 + \lambda)$. Wiener with a flat spectrum is $H^* G/(|H|^2 + S_n/S_f)$. They agree when $\lambda = S_n/S_f = 1/\mathrm{SNR}$.
:::
